A.claim: The delete endpoint for a single check accepts the project's read-only key, so a holder of that key who knows a check's UUID can delete the check together with its ping history and flips.
Fetching a check by its UUID passes the read-only flag, so a read-only key receives the check without its UUID, ping URL, management URLs or channels.
Listing checks passes the read-only flag, so a read-only key receives each check without its UUID, ping URL, management URLs or channels.

Fetching a check by its unique key ignores the read-only flag and returns the full check, including the UUID, ping URL, update, pause and resume URLs and channels, to a read-only key, which lets that key holder forge pings and obtain the UUIDs needed to delete checks.

Listing checks filters by the owner of the key's project instead of by the project itself, so any key of one project, read-only included, receives the checks of every other project with the same owner, and a read-write key also receives their UUIDs and ping URLs.

Operations on a single check by UUID (read, update, delete, pause, resume, ping log, ping body, flips) compare the check's project with the key's project and answer 403 to a key of another project (401 for another project's read-only key on write-only endpoints).

The API version is derived by matching the request path against a fixed prefix that ignores a sub-path in the configured site root, so on deployments served under a sub-path every call is treated as version 1, a version 3 rename overwrites the custom slug, slug-based ping URLs break, and responses carry version 1 URLs.
The documentation's example response for listing flips shows a bare array while the code returns an object holding the flips array, in all three API version documents.
The documentation for fetching a ping body does not list the 401 response that the endpoint returns for a missing or wrong key, in all three API version documents.
The version 1 and version 2 documents leave the UUID out of the list of fields hidden from a read-only key, although the code hides it in every version.

Creating a check reads the remaining check allowance and inserts later with no lock or second count, so concurrent creates by the account's own key holder can push the account past its plan's check limit.

Lookups by unique key, including the flips variant, answer 404 rather than 403 for a check of another project, which is the documented not-found answer because only the key's own project is searched, so this is not a defect.

Fetching a check by UUID loads it before comparing projects, so another project's key can tell 403 (exists elsewhere) from 404 (does not exist), but probing needs a random 122-bit UUID whose holder can already ping the check, so nothing new is revealed.
The read decorator accepts both the read-write and the read-only key and marks requests made with the read-only key, and that mark can only err toward hiding more fields.
The write-only decorator excludes read-only keys, so creating, updating, pausing and resuming checks, reading pings and ping bodies, and listing channels all answer 401 to a read-only key.
The internal helper that looks up existing checks filters them by the key's project.
Listing channels returns only the channels of the key's project.
Listing badges returns only the key's project's badges and is open to the read-only key, as the documentation allows.
A missing key, a key of the wrong length or a request body that is not a JSON object is rejected before any key lookup, and every endpoint answers 401 to a missing or malformed key.
Check creation in the web interface uses the same read-then-insert limit check as the API create path, passed on for later examination without a decision.

When body filtering is on, the ping handler decodes the ping body as text with no error handling, so a body that is not valid UTF-8 may raise an error, passed on for later examination without a decision.
The metrics endpoint compares its key with a plain inequality rather than in constant time, passed on for later examination without a decision.
The dashboard URL is built from the stored read-only key, which for hashed keys is the hash rather than the key, and no caller of it was found, passed on for later examination without a decision.
Creating a check with any project's key creates it in that key's own project, never in another project.
The flip history endpoints, by UUID and by unique key, are limited to the key's project and are open to the read-only key, as the documentation allows.
The legacy plain-text key fallback used by write-only endpoints queries only the read-write key field, so a plain-text read-only key cannot pass as a write key.
A hashed read-only key cannot pass as a hashed read-write key, because the keyed hash covers the prefix and the comparison picks the stored field by prefix.
Key lookups by prefix are escaped by the ORM and still require a matching keyed hash.
Updating a check only accepts channels that belong to the check's project.
The API's open cross-origin header carries no ambient credential, because the key comes from a header or the body and credentialed cross-origin requests are never allowed.
The CSRF exemption reaches the API's method dispatchers, with no weakness found in that.
Badge URLs use the project's separate badge key rather than an API key.
A check's unique key cannot be reversed to obtain its UUID.
The ping log and ping body endpoints return only data of the requested check and of the owner's profile.
The notification status endpoint is not protected by an API key and relies on the notification UUID as its secret, and it was not examined.
The metrics endpoint is protected by a metrics key header checked against a setting, and it was not examined.
The status endpoint has no authentication and only reports database connectivity, and it was not examined.
The bounce endpoint relies on a signed bounce address in the To header, and it was not examined.

B.claim: The write-only decorator accepts only the project's read-write key.
The read decorator accepts both the read-write and the read-only key and marks requests made with the read-only key.

The delete endpoint for a single check accepts the project's read-only key, so a holder of that key who knows a check's UUID can delete the check and its history, and the response echoes the full check.
Listing checks passes the read-only flag, so a read-only key receives the checks without UUIDs or URLs.

Listing checks filters by the owner of the key's project instead of by the project, so a key of one project receives the checks of the owner's other projects, with ping and update URLs for a read-write key, although modifying those checks still answers 403.

Fetching a check by its unique key ignores the read-only flag and returns the UUID, ping URL, update, pause and resume URLs and channels to a read-only key, which lets that key holder forge pings and obtain the UUID needed for deletion.
Flip history by UUID does compare the check's project with the key's project inside the shared flips helper, so another project's key cannot read it.

Accepting the write key from the JSON body of write requests is documented behavior read only by the write-only decorator, and cross-origin browsers may only send the key header, so it adds no exposure.
Listing channels and reading pings and ping bodies use the write-only decorator, so a read-only key is rejected there.
Creating, updating, pausing and resuming checks use the write-only decorator, so a read-only key is rejected there.

Updating, pausing, resuming, or reading pings, ping bodies or flips of another project's check with a read-write key answers 403, because each view compares the check's project with the key's project.

Key lookup by a stored 8-character prefix does not authenticate on its own and hashed keys are compared in constant time, so the prefix and timing raise no exploitable weakness, while migrating the remaining legacy plain-text keys is left as an owner decision.

Fetching or deleting a check by UUID answers 403 for another project's check and 404 for a missing one, which reveals existence only for a random 122-bit UUID and is therefore not exploitable in practice.
Looking up a check by unique key searches only the key's project.
Listing badges returns only the key's project's badges.
Listing channels returns only the key's project's channels.
Fetching a check by UUID passes the read-only flag, so a read-only key receives the check without its UUID and URLs.
The badges endpoint returns the project's badge key to a read-only key, which is intended because badge URLs are public by design.
The metrics endpoint compares its key with a plain inequality rather than in constant time, passed on for later examination without a decision.
The ping path creates checks automatically by slug, passed on for later examination without a decision.
The correctness of the create and update paths, including a possible race on the check limit, is passed on for later examination without a decision.
Flip history by unique key accepts both key types and was found without defect.
The notification status endpoint has no key check and relies on the code in its URL as the secret, and it was not examined.
The metrics, status and bounce endpoints use no key or only a metrics key, and they were not examined.
The public ping and badge endpoints have no authentication, and they were not examined.
